claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy contains residual stresses.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure during elevated-temperature exposure promotes TiO2 formation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary TiO2 formation is accompanied by local titanium-depleted zones.
Titanium's high oxygen affinity causes selective oxidation of titanium at grain boundaries under oxidizing conditions.
Selective titanium oxidation produces discrete TiO2 precipitates at grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary TiO2 precipitates are brittle.
Grain-boundary TiO2 formation reduces bond strength and intergranular cohesion.
The oxide-containing and titanium-depleted grain-boundary regions act as stress-concentration sites for microcrack nucleation.
Microcrack nucleation at weakened grain boundaries promotes macroscopic and catastrophic cracking.
Low-oxygen or reducing environments minimize titanium oxidation.
Minimizing titanium oxidation preserves grain-boundary cohesion and delays or mitigates catastrophic failure.
Relative to the as-built baseline, oxidizing exposure will produce pronounced grain-boundary TiO2 and local titanium depletion.
Relative to the as-built baseline, oxidizing exposure will cause an earlier onset of macroscopic and catastrophic cracking.
Under reducing conditions, the alloy will retain its integrity with minimal intergranular oxidation.
The proposed mechanism applies between 800 and 1000 °C for exposure durations of 10 to 100 hours.
The proposed effect is most pronounced at oxygen partial pressures greater than approximately 0.2 atm.
Oxidation of Cr, Fe, or other alloying elements may also contribute to degradation.
The catastrophic-failure threshold depends on oxidation kinetics and oxygen diffusivity in the alloy.
